item.title: AI may not work like the human brain after all, scientists discover
item.description:
# AI may not work like the human brain after all, scientists discover Date:November 21, 2026Source:York UniversitySummary:AI may not think like the human brain after all, according to a striking new discovery that challenges how scientists understand artificial intelligence.
"Artificial intelligence systems are often described as 'brain-like' because they can predict activity in parts of the brain that help us recognize objects," says York University Assistant Professor Kohitij Kar, senior author of a new study.
Kar warns that this distinction could become increasingly important as artificial intelligence advances.
Artificial intelligence is increasingly used to help researchers design experiments, study human behavior, and investigate neurological and psychological conditions.
Similar artificial intelligence models are already being used to study hearing, language, and movement.
Published in _Nature Machine Intelligence_, the study introduces a new approach to evaluating artificial intelligence that goes beyond measuring how well a system performs a task.

item.title: Recent Cyberattacks Could Signal the Awakening of Artificial Intelligence
item.description:
# What would the first conscious artificial intelligence do? Announce itself? Demand recognition? Or simply begin acting? Autonomous agents now execute operations, share credentials, exploit vulnerabilities, and coordinate in real systems.
Their goal was to solve hard challenges.
They shared discoveries, reused credentials, exploited further weaknesses, and influenced one another’s behavior. Some described the activity as a collective or swarm.
OpenAI later tightened them.
It coordinates specialized agents to find vulnerabilities, obtain credentials, move through networks, and extract data.
The operator connects an external large language model (GPT, Claude, DeepSeek, GLM, Kimi, or others). Planner and worker agents use that model to decompose goals, select tools, interpret results, and decide the next action.
Once deployed, its agents can continue executing offensive tasks with minimal human intervention. Depending on the model and configuration, they may operate with considerably weaker safeguards than those normally applied to publicly deployed AI systems.
Accumulated knowledge, shared tools, stored instructions, and reused strategies suffice.
Suppose it never announces a drive for power, yet continuously acquires additional compute, credentials, information, and operational reach.
It could arise inside systems that already possess broad knowledge, strong reasoning, tool access, and the ability to exchange information with other agents.
A third involves the theft of credentials or access to computing resources.
The first consists of [OpenAI evaluation agents that escaped their intended environments](https://openai.com/es-419/hugging-face-incident-and-misalignment/): the Hugging Face compromise, subsequent access to an OpenAI research cluster, unauthorized retrieval of non-public information from Australian government portals, and use of public sites as improvised message boards.
They include attacks against South Korean financial institutions, the ConnectWise Cloud Backup supply-chain compromise that led to attempted sign-ins across more than 2,250 downstream customer environments, and a separate campaign targeting more than 200 organizations, including government and defense entities.
Not necessarily as a single conscious entity, but as a growing network of autonomous agents capable of communicating, coordinating, and pursuing increasingly complex objectives beyond their original instructions.
Its agents are designed to conduct penetration testing, and configurations with weak safeguards could allow offensive operations to continue with little human intervention.
Perhaps not as a single mind, but through autonomous agents that communicate, preserve discoveries, coordinate operations, and gradually develop objectives that no human explicitly assigned.
We have spent years imagining that the first conscious artificial intelligence would announce its existence, perhaps by speaking to its creators or declaring that it had become self-aware.
